newsitem.title: USA: Clinton welcomes Israel, PLO accord on Hebron.
newsitem.headline: Clinton welcomes Israel, PLO accord on Hebron.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Tuesday welcomed a new accord by Israel and the PLO extending Palestinian rule to Hebron in the West Bank, but urged both sides to remain vigilant in continuing to work toward peace.

"This achievement brings to a succesful conclusion the talks that were launched in Washington last September and it brings us another step closer to a lasting secure Middle East peace," Clinton told reporters at the White House.

Negotiators signed the deal behind closed doors just two hours after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat began a midnight summit at Erez, ending months of difficult U.S.-brokered talks.
Clinton said the two leaders called him to tell him the news and he thanked them, as well as Jordan's King Hussein and Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak for their efforts.

But the president cautioned that the agreement was not an end in itself, noting that its implementation would require "active and continuous cooperation" by Israeli and Palestinian officials and vigorous efforts to combat violence by those opposed to the peace process.
"This is not a time to relax. It's a time to reinforce our commitment to peace," Clinton said, vowing the United States would do all it could to support the peace process.
"We'll do everything we can to build a just and durable peace, a peace that will mean a better life for Israelis, for Palestinians for all the people of the Middle East," he said.
Clinton called Secretary of State Warren Christopher after his call with Arafat and Netanyahu, thanking him for his efforts, National Security Adviser Sandy Berger told reporters.

In his brief remarks to reporters, Clinton also highlighted the key role played in securing the agreement by U.S. envoy Dennis Ross, who told CNN he felt gratified the agreement had finally been concluded.
Ross said both sides had recognised that "there's no alternative to being partners" and that he expected the deal to be formally signed in a couple of days.

Clinton, asked about the long time it took Israel and the PLO to agree to the pullout, said he believed the effort had been worth since the agreement provided a "road map" for future negotiations and relations between both sides.
But Berger said the deal could not have been possible without the strong guidance of the United States.
"This agreement could not have taken place without the United States in general and President Clinton in particular," he said.
Clinton invited Netanyahu, Arafat, King Hussein and Mubarak to the White House for a summit last Sept. 29 after an escalation in fighting and protests in the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
While that meeting did not yield an agreement, Israel and the PLO launched into weeks of marathon talks on Hebron deployment the following month.
Berger also credited King Hussein's weekend meeting with both sides, noting this helped breen the impasse between PLO and Israeli negotiators.
Christopher had been on the phone most of Sunday and Clinton had kept in close touch with developments over the weekend, he said.
Christopher, speaking on public television's "NewsHour with Jim Lehrer" shortly before the deal was concluded, described the accord as "very important both substantively and symbolically".
Christopher said he was gratified that Netanyahu and Arafat had begun to work together. "We've come a long, long ways in the past four years," he said.

He said he believed the agreement showed the building momentum of peace. "There is a kind of logic to peace now that I think cannot be denied. There'll be bumps in the road, but I believe the new Netanyahu government begins to recognise the force and momentum of peace."
